summary: Describes a simple extension to TFTP, the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, that lets a client and server negotiate options before a transfer begins. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Before swapping a file, the two computers quickly agree on how they will do it, like deciding the size of the boxes.

questions: what is a tftp oack packet
how does tftp blksize negotiation work
subtitle: How a TFTP client and server agree on transfer options before any file data moves.

tldr.problem: TFTP is a simple lock-step file transfer protocol with no way for the two ends to agree on how a transfer should work before it starts.
tldr.mechanism: The client appends option/value pairs to its Read or Write Request. A server that understands them answers with a new Option Acknowledgment (OACK) packet listing the options it accepts.
tldr.outcome: Options can be negotiated in a backward-compatible way: a server that knows nothing about options just ignores them and the transfer proceeds as plain TFTP. The RFC obsoletes RFC 1782 and updates RFC 1350.

today: RFC 2347 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1782 and updates RFC 1350. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Backward-Compatible Extension
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP, RFC 1350) is a simple, lock-step protocol that lets a client get a file from, or put a file onto, a remote host. RFC 2347 adds a way to negotiate options before the transfer starts.

The mechanism reuses TFTP's own Request packet format and keeps a request-respond-acknowledge sequence, similar to TFTP's own lock-step approach. It is general purpose, but it was created to support the Blocksize option defined in RFC 2348. More options are defined in RFC 2349.
sections.eli5: TFTP is a very simple way to hand a file across, one piece at a time. This RFC adds a short chat at the start so both sides can agree on the details.

sections.title: Options on Request Packets
sections.content:
Options are appended to the end of a Read Request or Write Request packet. The packet keeps its usual fields: the opcode (1 for a Read Request, 2 for a Write Request), the filename and the mode (netascii, octet or mail). After these come any number of option and value pairs.

Every field is NULL-terminated. Option names and values are written in case-insensitive ASCII, for example blksize. The order of options is not significant, and an option may only be given once. The maximum size of a request packet is 512 octets.
sections.eli5: It is like writing a note on the bottom of a request form: 'and please use big boxes'. Each wish is written as a name and a value.

sections.title: The Option Acknowledgment Packet
sections.content:
A new packet type, the Option Acknowledgment (OACK), has opcode 6. It carries the option and value pairs the server accepts, each NULL-terminated. Each option is copied from the original request, and the value is the acknowledged value.

Whether and how the acknowledged value may differ from the requested one is described in the specification of each individual option. The RFC also defines a new error code, 8, used to say that a transfer should be terminated because of option negotiation.
sections.eli5: The OACK is the reply note: 'Yes, I can do these things you asked for.' It only repeats wishes it agrees to.

sections.title: How Negotiation Works
sections.content:
Only the client may start negotiation. If the server supports options and recognizes at least one in the request, it may respond with an OACK containing each option it recognizes and accepts the value for. The server must not include any option the client did not request. Options it does not support should be left out of the OACK and should not cause an ERROR packet. If the value of a supported option is invalid, that option's own specification says whether to omit it, answer with an alternate value, or send an ERROR with error code 8.

An option the server did not acknowledge must be ignored by both sides as if it was never requested. A client must use the acknowledged options and must not use the others.

For a Read Request the server can answer with an OACK (options accepted), a DATA packet (request accepted, options not) or an ERROR. For a Write Request the answers are OACK, ACK (request accepted, options not) or ERROR. A server without option support will likely ignore the extra data and reply with DATA or ACK as normal. If a server returns an error because of the options, the client may repeat the request without them.

The client confirms an OACK differently depending on the request. After a Read Request it sends an ACK with block number 0. After a Write Request it simply starts with the first DATA packet using the negotiated values. A client that rejects the OACK sends an ERROR with error code 8, which ends the transfer. The same applies if the OACK contains an option the client never requested.
sections.eli5: The asker makes wishes and the other side only says yes to the ones it understands. Anything it did not say yes to is forgotten, and if it does not understand wishes at all, the transfer goes ahead the plain way.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows a read of foofile in octet mode with blksize 1432. The server replies with an OACK repeating blksize 1432, the client sends an ACK for block 0, and the server then sends DATA blocks of 1432 octets, each acknowledged. The last block is shorter than 1432 octets.

A write of barfile with blksize 2048 follows the other pattern: after the OACK the client goes straight to DATA packets of 2048 octets, and the server answers each with an ACK.
sections.eli5: For a download, the client says 'okay, go' with a zero-numbered thank-you. For an upload, the client just starts sending.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Basic TFTP has no security mechanism. This is why it has no rename, delete or file overwrite capabilities. This document does not add any security to TFTP, but the RFC states that the extensions do not add any additional security risks.
sections.eli5: TFTP has no locks, and this change does not add any, but it does not make things more risky either.
